analysis.one_liner: Restores the FCC's 2010 net neutrality rules struck down by a federal court, until the FCC writes new ones.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past a Senate committee referral; it was introduced in February 2014, sent to the Commerce Committee, and died there when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In January 2014 a federal court struck down the FCC's 2010 'open Internet' rules, which required broadband providers to treat all web traffic equally. Senator Markey's bill would have put those rules back into force until the FCC finished writing replacements. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday internet users, small websites, startups, and online businesses. The bill would have kept broadband providers from legally charging websites for faster delivery or blocking and slowing content, keeping the internet open to anyone who can publish or build a service online. Consumers would be protected from paid fast lanes that could eventually raise prices or degrade service for the sites and apps they use.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users, startups, and small websites

how_it_helps.text: Restores the FCC's vacated 2010 open Internet rules, which barred broadband providers from blocking lawful content and required transparency about network management practices.

Keeps those rules in effect until the FCC takes final action on the replacement rules the court's decision required it to write, closing the gap during which broadband providers would face no anti-blocking or anti-discrimination rules.
Preserves the FCC's ability to enforce penalties against violations that occurred during that period even after new rules take effect.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers such as cable, telephone, and wireless internet companies. The vacated rules limited their ability to charge online services for prioritized 'fast lane' access, block or slow competing services, and manage traffic without disclosure. If enforcement of those rules later proved to require common-carrier-style regulation, providers could also face heavier regulatory obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable, phone, and wireless broadband providers

drawbacks.text: The bill is a temporary patch, not a lasting policy: it simply reinstates rules a court already ruled the FCC lacked proper legal authority to impose, leaving the underlying legal problem to the FCC's remand proceedings.

Broadband providers argue that heavy network management and usage-based capacity planning are necessary to keep networks running, and a blanket restoration of the vacated rules gives them no room to negotiate paid arrangements that might help fund network investment.
Rules that courts vacate can create regulatory uncertainty for providers planning billion-dollar network investments, since the legal ground could shift again once the FCC writes new rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary internet users the benefit is real but modest in scope: it would restore protections against blocking and discrimination during a transition period, not create a permanent open-internet regime. The main cost falls on broadband providers' flexibility to charge web companies for prioritized access. The bill's weakness is that it restores rules the courts had already said were legally shaky, so even a win would have been temporary; the real fight was always over what permanent rules the FCC would write next.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the Open Internet Preservation Act on February 3, 2014, weeks after the D.C. Circuit's Verizon v. FCC decision vacated the FCC's 2010 open Internet rules.
Six Democratic senators — Udall of New Mexico, Blumenthal, Franken, Wyden, Merkley, and Markey — cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which took no further action on it.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still sitting in committee, and all bills not passed by then die automatically.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers benefited from the bill's death: the vacated 2010 rules stayed off the books while the FCC weighed its next move, leaving them without binding anti-blocking or anti-discrimination rules during the gap period the bill was designed to cover.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to restore the FCC's vacated net neutrality rules.

for.name: 6 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: Udall (NM), Blumenthal, Franken, Wyden, Merkley, and Markey.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or vote on it.

against.name: Broadband and telecom industry
against.role: Cable, telephone, and wireless internet providers
against.what_they_did: Opposed restoration of the vacated 2010 open Internet rules, which their court challenge had just struck down, and lobbied against legislative reinstatement.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters — the sponsor and six cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored or took recorded action on the bill.

industries.industry: Broadband providers (cable, telephone, and wireless ISPs)
industries.note: The bill would have put back the 2010 rules barring them from blocking lawful content and required them to disclose network management, the same rules they had just succeeded in vacating in court. It also constrained their ability to charge websites for priority delivery, a potential new revenue stream.

Restored rules would keep web companies from having to pay broadband providers for fast-lane access or worry about being blocked or throttled, preserving their ability to reach users without gatekeeper tolls.
The rules protected internet users' access to lawful content and required providers to be transparent about how they manage their networks.
